articles.title: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism
articles.summary: Netflix documentary Primetime Preacher$ travels back to a time when evangelism found a dominant place on US television – and the shocking tabloid stories that followed.
body: For three decades, film-maker Joe Berlinger has gripped true-crime buffs with his deep dives into small-town murders and infamous serial killers. His Netflix explorations of John Wayne Gacy and Jeffrey Dahmer helped flip documentary storytelling from viewer homework to a welcome distraction.

After dedicating so much time to the life of Jeffrey Epstein, the kidnapping of JonBenét Ramsey and other unsolved mysteries, Berlinger thought Primetime Preacher$, his new Netflix documentary on America’s televangelist boom, would offer a break. But it turns out that’s a pretty juicy crime story too, about the religious right’s bank job on American politics. “The deeper resonance for me came when I realized that the global televangelism rise actually mirrors the rise of the religious right,” he says. “Religion and politics, from Reagan on, has really changed politics for the worse in my opinion. This was the birth of that.”

articles.title: Kylian Mbappé Impersonator Leads Colorful Roster of Doubles in Egyptian Doc ‘The Lookalike’
articles.summary: The growing commotion on the streets near a soccer stadium would easily lead one to believe superstar player Kylian Mbappé himself was signing fan autographs. But, as seen in “The Lookalike,” the furore was not over the French player, but a charismatic impersonator.
body: When asked about the inspiration for the project, Elkoussi tells Variety she grew up seeing Mounir impersonators, but was struck by stumbling upon one of her film’s subjects on social media and realizing he did dozens of concerts a month and had built a career around his resemblance to the star. “That was when the idea really clicked into focus: how do these lookalikes become a stand-in for the real star? What drives that? How do they draw in a big audience that sees in them a star within reach? What drives the audience that creates this kind of stardom for them?”

The director first began developing the project in August of 2024, going on to film for eight months between 2025 and 2026. The experience of following the lookalikes and trying to understand people’s fascination with them came with several “surprises” for the filmmaker.

“I was surprised by the smiles on kids’ faces in the streets whenever they ran into the Mbappé lookalike, reacting as if they were standing right in front of the real Mbappé,” she recalls. “I was surprised by how seriously the Mbappé lookalike took his work, and how committed [he is] as a content creator.”

articles.title: An Iranian Woman Falls Pregnant to Avoid Execution in ‘Inherited’: Situation in Iran Is ‘Increasingly Complex’
articles.summary: A few years ago, Iranian filmmaker Morteza Alizadeh saw a photograph that he couldn’t shake from his mind: it showed mothers and their children going about their lives, which at first seemed routine, until the director realized it was taken inside a women’s prison.
body: “My main goal with this film was to portray people who find themselves in difficult and sensitive situations, where they are forced to make choices to survive,” Alizadeh tells Variety. “These choices affect not only their own lives but, more importantly, the lives of others.”

The director dedicated a long period to research, collecting an extensive archive of images from inside prisons, which included rare documentaries and footage from hacked surveillance cameras. He also spent months meeting and interviewing women who had been imprisoned and had either been released temporarily or were on leave. “With their help, we were able to design the entire prison environment in detail,” he notes. “Then our production design team recreated and built the whole prison set as closely as possible to the real thing.”

By posing a complex moral conundrum when Mina’s family pleads with the unmarried prisoner to abort the baby to preserve the family’s honor, the director wanted the audience to “ask themselves” how much right “does one person have to decide another person’s fate.” “What gives us the authority to decide whether to take someone’s life or give another person the chance to live?”

articles.title: ‘The Blind Ferryman’ Director on Rejecting Western Stereotypes: ‘I Don’t Want to Make a Movie Asking for Sympathy’
articles.summary: For Iraqi-Swiss filmmaker Ali Toffan Al-Fatlawi, the idea behind “The Blind Ferryman” began with a thought that struck him during Iraq’s civil war in 2006. Living in Switzerland and watching the violence unfold in his homeland, he thought of two of his aunts who were blind and found himself wishing…
body: Set in Iraq’s southern marshlands, the film follows Ayoub (Ahmed Moneka), a blind boatman who falls in love with Genya (Sam Rahmani), a mysterious woman whom nobody else can see. Convinced she exists only in his imagination, his community mocks him, forcing Ayoub to defend a love in which only he believes.
“When you love someone, why do you need the agreement of other people?” Al-Fatlawi asks. “It’s your love, it’s your own decision.”

The character of Genya draws on stories Al-Fatlawi heard from his father about a mythical woman who appeared to men in the marshlands, as well as ancient Sumerian mythology and the “Epic of Gilgamesh.” The filmmaker was particularly fascinated by the prominence of female deities in ancient Mesopotamian mythology, questioning how those figures gave way to the predominantly male image of God that characterizes contemporary religion.

The marshlands themselves were equally important to his vision. Beyond their mythical associations, they offered Al-Fatlawi an opportunity to portray a side of Iraq rarely seen on screen, challenging the familiar images of war, poverty and destruction that have long dominated international representations of the country.

articles.title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
articles.summary: For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful? • This article does not contain major spoilers.
body: Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there.

Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding.

You Can See Everything acts as if this isn’t the case. It operates in a realm of smart and artful naivety. In order to interrogate whether or not Elizabeth Holmes, founder of magical medical tech company Theranos, is – as she claims – the tragic victim of a miscarriage of justice, Nathan Fielder moves into the annexe of her home for a few weeks before she starts her 11-year prison term for fraud.
points: For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception.
Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real.

articles.title: Obese Monkey Becomes a Weight-Loss Drug Guinea Pig in ‘Boltrim’ at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar
articles.summary: Director Ashish Aryan is presenting “Boltrim,” a Hindi-English dark comedy about an obese monkey subjected to drug trials by a pharmaceutical giant developing a weight-loss injection, to the Co-Production Market at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar.
body: An NFDC Screenwriters’ Lab alum (“T for Taj Mahal”), Aryan has previously produced and written the web series “Matka King” (Prime Video), and directed “Roti, Kapda & Internet” (“Bread, Butter & Internet”). The idea for “Boltrim” came from a news report about a global shortage of laboratory monkeys, which had driven prices up to $50,000 per animal.

“I was drawn to the disturbing intersection of two worlds – the smuggling and exploitation of animals in an increasingly lucrative clinical-trial industry, and our own obsession with bodily perfection, which a loss-making pharma company decides to capitalize on,” Aryan says. “Weight-loss injections meant to treat obesity and diabetes are now being widely used as a cosmetic shortcut. I want to explore how much cruelty we are willing to overlook in the pursuit of looking perfect.”

The Writers Cloud, Jugaad Motion Pictures and Mirage Films are attached to the project, with $320,000 of its $1.2 million budget secured. Producer Siddartha Jatla (Busan title “Love and Shukla”) says the team is seeking international co-production and platform partners in Europe and Asia.

body: We're just weeks away from Christmas but for many music fans their thoughts have already turned to next summer's festival season.
Glastonbury announced its line-up this week, tickets are on sale for Reading and Leeds and the headliners for Belladrum have been announced.

articles.title: The film about fencing set between two cultures
articles.summary: Parvinder Shergill talks about creating art that honours both of her cultural backgrounds.
body: It was Hollywood more than Bollywood that British Indian filmmaker Parvinder Shergill grew up on, with Karate Kid, Rocky, A Few Good Men and ET among her favourite films.
The actor, writer and producer, who lives in Berkshire, says she feels "really lucky" that she comes from "two worlds".
Shergill says she builds stories around both cultures, the latest of which are her new film Touché and her first play Threads of Healing.
As she talks about wanting to "inspire" with her work, she says "it's an exciting time to embrace who you are, whatever that means to you".

articles.title: Why Sylvester Stallone's Father In I Play Rocky Looks So Familiar
articles.summary: If Sylvester Stallone's father Frank looks familiar in I Play Rocky, it's because the actor behind him has a very long and impressive list of credits.
body: Peter Farrelly's biopic "I Play Rocky" tells the story of a young Sylvester Stallone (Anthony Ippolito) as he rises through his early, sketchy acting career, eventually coming to write and star in 1976's "Rocky," itself one of the best sports movies ever made. The film doesn't sugarcoat Stallone's early struggles, including his run-down apartment, his inability to land good roles as a young actor going by the name of Mike (leading him to work on an adult feature), and the fact that, at one point, he had to sleep on the street.

It also depicts the verbal abuse that he suffered at the hands of his domineering father, Frank Sr, who runs a barbershop and is hardly encouraging. When Stallone relates his acting dreams, Frank tells his son that he isn't handsome enough to be a movie star. Ouch, dad.
points: If Sylvester Stallone's father Frank looks familiar in I Play Rocky, it's because the actor behind him has a very long and impressive list of credits.

articles.title: Why is Blackpool such a Strictly highlight?
articles.summary: Strictly's annual visit to Blackpool has become synonymous with big staging and unforgettable shows.
body: From Halloween high kicks to magical Movie Week moves, Strictly Come Dancing's highlights can often come thick and fast, but once a season, there is a particular peculiarity that has become a much-loved tradition - the annual decamp to Blackpool.
The seaside resort was a location in the first series of the BBC programme back in 2004 and went on to become a mainstay moment.
The show returns to the town on Saturday and will see eight couples taking to the dancefloor in the magnificent Blackpool Tower Ballroom.
But how did Blackpool become such a Strictly highlight and what does it mean to the town?
